utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Judge Fluegge is, for urgent personal reasons, unable to hear the case with us today. Judge Moloto and myself have considered whether it would be in the interest of the -- interests of justice to continue to hear the case. We concluded that it was. We also had in mind that the expected absence of Judge Fluegge will be of short duration. We expect him to be back tomorrow. Therefore, we'll sit 15 bis today. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I would just like to introduce a lawyer to the team. I think you've seen her before. This is Sarah Melikian, one of our newer lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome to court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kralj. Before we continue, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. We'll now continue. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kralj.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask to have 1D2212 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, Mr. Kralj, this is a document of the Main Staff. The date is the 12th of February, 1994. At that time, you were still in the 1st Krajina Corps, weren't you? Can you tell us, on the basis of this document, whether we can see that the 1st Krajina Corps received the document that is before us? Have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows that the 1st Krajina Corps did receive this document and I was aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the introductory part of the document, the sources are referred to, and it says that is what is under way is a planned and organised action to provide the Muslims with military equipment, strategic materials, and other different equipment for waging war. Do you remember that you were aware of these findings of the VRS at the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were reports that humanitarian organisations were engaged in reconnaissance activity in addition to their regular activities. In order to prevent that or reduce that, this order was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 and further on, it says that the inspection of the same convoy two or more times is forbidden. Do you know whether that was carried out in practice?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases when some check-points tried to check convoys arbitrarily. This order did away with that, and it was strictly stated that a convoy could be checked only once after entering the territory of Republika Srpska and then, afterwards, they would cross the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we need the next page in the English version, paragraph 7. So we need the bottom of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says: "Avoid incidents, but if they occur, inform the VRS Main Staff immediately." In practice, were attempts made to avoid incidents with convoys?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 1st Krajina Corps, we strictly paid attention to that, not to have any kind of incidents whatsoever with convoys. Even more so, because the route from the entrance, from Gradiska to Turbe towards Zenica, was very long, and it went through this terrain where there could have been some groups or individuals who were just acting on their own who would ask convoys perhaps for some favours and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the next page in B/C/S. Let us focus on paragraph 8. The order says that the personnel of UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations should be treated professionally and politely. Then paragraph 9 says: "The corps command will assign a person in the corps command to follow the situation related to the movement of UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations in their zone and resolve problems."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your corps, who was in charge of this that is referred to in paragraph 9; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for paragraph number 9, the sector for civilian affairs was in charge of that, and I personally was in charge of that, as I was a member of that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D715, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D715 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 16 of your statement, you speak of certain cases when some convoys or parts of certain convoys were returned or were not allowed passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please see 1D2216 in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the Drina Corps, of the command of the Drina Corps, the 17th of September, 1993. And the Main Staff is supposed to receive this document and it is Colonel Magazin that is supposed to deal with this. Do you know who Colonel Magazin is?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Magazin was the chief of Department for Civilian Affairs in the Main Staff of VRS. Later on, Colonel Milos Djurdjic took over from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll count the lines. Line 9 from the middle in B/C/S, line 8 in the English version, what is written here is the following: "They did not allow the vehicle to be inspected," that is to say, the participants in the convoy didn't. Was it the duty of the persons accompanying the convoys to allow the inspection of convoys by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty of the escorts of convoys was to allow inspection by the VRS, according to the procedures carried out by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were UNPROFOR and the UNHCR informed, do you remember, that equipment for video recording was prohibited?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everyone had been informed in detail that equipment for video recording not was allowed, regardless of whether it is UNPROFOR or other humanitarian organisations, because they had appropriate meetings before they submitted requests for movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see from this document that members of the convoy had 35 cameras on them, and after the truck was stopped - the one that could not be inspected - the convoy proceeded towards Sarajevo. So what was the procedure when forbidden goods were found? Was there a right to keep the entire convoy, to stop it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was to inspect the convoy. If it was established that something was wrong or that there was something that was being smuggled, something that was not on the list, then an assessment was made. If it was ammunition or something more serious, then the entire convoy would be stopped. However, since these were goods that were not for military purposes, then such goods would be seized temporarily and returned subsequently, or in agreement with the leader of the convoy, it would be returned to the origin and what was all right would continue the journey. Of course, if the leader of the convoy would agree. In most cases, the leader of the convoy would agree and the convoy would continue its journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would tender this document into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D716, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D716 is admitted. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] And now I would like do call up 1D2215.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this document, which is dated 26 September 1993, in paragraph 3, it says that UNPROFOR activities in the territory of Republika Srpska are numerous. Every day on the roads there are very large numbers of UN Military Observer teams, civilian police, convoys to relieve forces in the demilitarised zone of Srebrenica and Zepa, logistical support convoys, and columns escorting convoys by humanitarian organisations and UNPROFOR command organs on reconnaissance and other activities. It also says that so far the most frequented routes are locations in the east of Republika Srpska as follows: Zepa, Srebrenica, Sarajevo. In the following paragraph, there's a reference to a systematic gathering of information on the situation in the territory. And then there is reference to much recording done with video cameras and still cameras, that there are people deliberately stopping in the sectors where VRS and MUP positions and check-points are located. It also says that columns halt on the roads at will. They deliberately run late and travel after dark. They stay overnight in RS territory without anybody's knowledge and approval, and so on. In conclusion, it says that all those activities are for the purpose of intelligence and reconnaissance activities. My question is: Was UNPROFOR allowed to halt, to stop by the positions of the VRS without being announced, to spend a night in the VRS territory without anybody's knowledge or approval?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not receive English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] UNPROFOR was not allowed to spend any time in Republika Srpska, according to its mandate. They were only allowed to pass through the territory of Republika Srpska providing they were previously announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Judges did receive the interpretation of this part of your answer. Was there anything else you wanted to add?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to underscore that according to UNPROFOR's mandate, they were not allowed to stay in the territory of Republika Srpska. All of their movements had to be announced and controlled by the military of Republika Srpska in keeping with agreements that were reached between UNPROFOR, the command of the Army of Republika Srpska, and the command of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're interested in the following page in both versions. Paragraph 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says that: "We know for certain that all VRS firing positions, anti-aircraft defence rocket unit positions, air surveillance and warning system positions, command posts, communication centres, central hubs have been detected and recorded." When it comes to the gathering of those data, was that agreed with the VRS or was it done in secret by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The data in question was gathered secretly by UNPROFOR. They wanted to assess the situation as it was on the VRS side. Later on, it would turn out that the data collected was also used for other purposes. To be more specific, for air-strike campaigns.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the following paragraph, it says that NATO forces have carried out deployment and trained and drilled their guidance officers. Had that been agreed with VRS?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that such a detrimental activity cannot be agreed or approved. And as for guidance forces, they guide missiles to be precise in bombarding particular facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 8 it says that: "It is not unusual for columns from UNPROFOR or humanitarian organisations to openly oppose a planned inspection when entering RS territory." In such cases, those convoys which did not allow control, were they allowed to enter the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally had a problem at the Gradiska border crossing. A UNHCR convoy arrived from the direction of Zagreb. We had organised a somewhat more detailed control of its cargo but it wasn't allowed. After the convoy leader consulted with his superior in Zagreb, we agreed that the convoy would go back to Zagreb because they wouldn't allow us to control it. Later on, we learned that that same convoy went in the direction of Bihac and that it carried a certain quantity of weapons and ammunition in covered spaces within the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it agreed that such convoys --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could we seek clarification. You said you later learned. How did you learn that, that there was a certain quantity of weapons and ammunition was hidden in the covered spaces? How did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The intelligence organs recorded statements by logistics organs in Bihac, and they claimed that a certain quantity of weapons and ammunition was received through UNHCR convoys, and this matched our data on the movement of that convoy which had been stopped and returned to Zenica across Banja Luka and Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if such recordings would be available, that, of course, would assist the Chamber in better understanding what is now presented as a rather general way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The document, this document is pretty specific so I don't think that evidence in general is general. It's very specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the document which the witness is talking about. That it was recorded. Because then we have one focussed situation and that allows also for -- to see whether there's any -- whether there's any protest or -- against such allegations. That's -- but if it's there, do not hesitate to present it. If it's not there, then, of course, we'll have to do without. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kralj, where would we be able to find that document? You say that the security organ recorded the conversations of their logistics organs in which they mentioned that they received weapons from UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. One second. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. I think we've got an important translation problem. I think I heard that Colonel Kralj said he received intelligence information and the question went back to him as security information. So I think if we could make sure that we've got the same units being talked to -- about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please understand the question such, Mr. Kralj, that Mr. Lukic was seeking information on where such recordings made by intelligence organs were kept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this can be found here in e-court, because in previous cases, it was mentioned that that convoy transported weapons. That is mentioned in some reports that were presented, and they refer to logistics reports from Bihac. According to them, the only aid that they received was from UNHCR. Later on, I put two and two together and I realised that it is about the same convoy, because the times matched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then in that case, could we be clear whether the colonel is getting his information from his time at the VRS or what he has learned over the years here as documents have been shown to him. It's a little -- now a little unclear to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you willing to follow the suggestion made by Mr. McCloskey to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, you heard my learned friend, Mr. McCloskey. He wants you to clarify and tell him what you knew before - if anything - and what you learned subsequently from documents, if you indeed learned anything from the documents subsequently shown to you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first part, it is true that the convoy did not allow us to control it and returned, and we had our doubts about the convoy's cargo. We thought that it was transporting weapons. And I -- as for the second part, I was shown some documents where a reference was made to the intelligence of the enemy side and their reports in which they say that they received weapons from UNHCR and that was the only assistance they had. Those weapons were transported in a UNHCR convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- When you say "we later learned," you later saw documents, is that at the time, well, let's say, within a short -- within a short period after you were there when the convoy was stopped; or is it that you saw those documents and you received that information later? That means after the war, for example, in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I established that here at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you also -- that reports in which they say that they received weapons from UNHCR, earlier you told us that -- that was one of your conclusions, that the documents did not literally say that, but that you matched the information and that you concluded that weapons were provided by UNHCR. Is it that the documents directly state that weapons were received by the UNHCR; or is it that matching the information made you conclude that they were sent by UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I read that they were received from UNHCR in Bihac, that a certain quantity of ammunition and weapons were received there. And I concluded that that was one and the same convoy that was supposed to cross the border from Gradiska and then continue on to Banja Luka and Zenica. It never went through there. It repeated its journey, but the second time round, it passed through Bihac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, the documents are explicit in that weapons and ammunition was provided by UNHCR, and you concluded that that must have been the same convoy as you had seen before, which then later provided that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- material. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] We would tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we at least see who wrote it or whose name it was under?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we see the last page on both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see the name of Manojlo Milovanovic typed out here. Would you say that that is customary for General Milovanovic to be dealing with this kind of work?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Milovanovic was in charge of such affairs, and he did send these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that with this information there's no further objection, Mr. McCloskey? Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D717, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D717 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have 1D2220, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have before us a rather short document. It is a document of the Main Staff dated the 21st of March, 1995, signed by General Milovanovic. It says -- actually, military post codes 7111 and 7598 are being provided with information to the effect that the medical evacuation from Srebrenica to Sarajevo is being authorised on the 22nd of March, 1995. First of all, at that time, were you at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I was at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether medical evacuations were allowed from the area of Srebrenica, Zepa, Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medical evacuations were allowed, and they were not subjected to the 48-hour notification in advance. They were carried out in two ways: Either by land or by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D718, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D718 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter number 24650, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see another short document here. The date is the 4th of February, 1995. It's a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. It was signed by Colonel Milivoj Miletic, and the UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo is being informed that medical evacuation from Gorazde has been allowed. At the time, were you a member of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Main Staff at the time. And if you allow me, just one correction. It is not Milivoj Miletic, it is Radivoje Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry if I misspoke. Were you aware of such evacuations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of such evacuations and the position that this had to be resolved urgently. It had priority in relation to other matters related to convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D719, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D719 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would ask now for 65 ter number 24689.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've already mentioned that evacuations took place by helicopter as well. We see a document here dated the 13th of February, 1995. It was signed by General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we only see a B/C/S version on our screen. Is an English translation uploaded? There seems to be no English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Hmm. I'm not aware that English translation is missing, but since it's short document, I'll just read one sentence and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I add one thing. Is there a dispute about - now and then, I'm not talking about the frequency - that medical evacuations took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The evidence suggests now and then medical evacuations did take place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So, therefore, the issue is then whether they responded to the needs or whether the frequency was such that it could be considered either co-operative or obstructive rather than whether individual incidents of medical evacuation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In this time-period that's correct. As we get into, as you know, closer to the Srebrenica time-period specifics are more relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Lukic, therefore what you're establishing now in the various documents, there seems to be no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then I'll just tender this one for MFI, to be MFI'd, and I will move on from this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D720, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D720 is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, in relation to what Judge Orie said, were you aware of any medical evacuations being refused? Do you know of any such example?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any medical evacuations being refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we have 1D2223 on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a document of the command of the Drina Corps here, and the date is the 2nd of May, 1994. This is a list of goods delivered by humanitarian organisations to the Muslims via the territory of Republika Srpska. On the right-hand side, it says April 1994, above that text that I just read out. So it says that seven convoys went to Srebrenica in that period of time. Seven convoys of the Swedish team with 98 trucks of construction material and equipment for prefabricated buildings. In the table, we see the type of goods involved, and we see what was sent to which zone. For example, flour: 1.769 tonnes were delivered to Tuzla; Srebrenica, 229 tonnes; Sarajevo, 63 tonnes; Zepa, 92 tonnes. Were you aware of this, that such lists were being made of goods delivered, delivered in the enclaves?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time that you are referring to, I was at the 1st Krajina Corps. We did keep records there, cumulative records, and when I came to the Main Staff, then I saw that in the documentation that was kept by Colonel Milos Djurdjic, there were such lists too. According to the towns where humanitarian aid had been delivered. Over a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Given the importance, I just wanted to note we have a typo on the year in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the left top corner, it says 1995, where the original says 1994, whereas to the right it says April 1994. Perhaps if would be good -- it's not really a translation issue but rather a transcription issue. Therefore, if a -- if a version which exclusively contains this correction could be uploaded, that would be preferable. I don't think we have to submit it entirely again to CLSS. It's a transcription issue rather than anything else. And perhaps it is a document which was -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's just the translation, the English version which would then reflect that the original says 1994, the left top corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we then MFI it before it's corrected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there is such a little chance that I would rather if you inform the Chamber or if Mr. -- I don't know where the document comes from. Is it -- is it the translation prepared by CLSS? Is it prepared through the Prosecution or at the request of the Defence? But the party which is most adequate to provide a revised version is invited to report to the Chamber once it's there so that we'll allow the Registrar to attach the new English version to the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll take care of that. I think it's our document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll hear from you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We'll tender the document for the admission, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I would -- under the present circumstance I would not oppose admission. There's -- especially it's the original, of course, which is the core of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now that Mr. McCloskey raised the question of precision, I see that on the original we've got on the left side 2nd of May, 1994. On the right side, April 1994. I'm not quite sure whether there is any dispute about the month and the exact date, but in light of the requirement for precision, I just want to make the parties aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that the period that was processed was April 1994. That's why the document is from the 2nd of May, the beginning of the next month. So the whole April is accounted for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That makes sense. If the Prosecution agrees. But if you do not agree, the original says that and we've heard how Mr. Lukic understands the document, that on the 2nd of May, a document was produced covering the month of April and -- 98 trucks of construction material, et cetera, as -- and 23 trucks for Gorazde. So we'll -- that's how you understand the document. Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D721, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D721 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would ask for 1D2231, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The previous document was a document of the Army of Republika Srpska. Now this document is from the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The 31st of March, 1995, and it's type signed, chief of defence department, Professor Suljo Hasanovic. And the subject is recording donations. In the text, it says: "We hereby send you an overview of the quantities of food, materiel, and technical equipment, and fuel issued to military units in our area for March 1995 ..." And then the actual quantities are listed. Next paragraph: "We add that the above quantities were allotted from a consignment of humanitarian aid which arrived in this area through the UNHCR and this is the only source of supply." Mr. Kralj, did you know, did you have any intelligence about the Muslim side taking humanitarian aid that was meant to be used by civilians and that they are distributing it to their own armed forces?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Milos Djurdjic was informed about humanitarian aid. Some of it was allocated to the army. It was on its way to Srebrenica. He informed me about that, so I knew that some of the humanitarian aid headed not only for that enclave but for others as well was distributed to the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see it's a break time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is. Mr. Kralj, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, are you on schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what we do as well. But we'd like to receive the information relevant to see whether our hope will become true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just have to check the time with Mr. Ram as well. But I think I'm on track.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're on track. I think yesterday you had close to 45 minutes. Today you used a little bit less than one hour at this moment, and you are scheduled for two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that, overall, you're coming close to one and a half hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm on track then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you're on track. So that means you need another half an hour or a little bit plus. We'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness is with us, I would -- I forgot to tender 1D2231.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D722, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D722 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the next document on our screens, we should have 1D2224.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, we have a new document in front of us. The document was issued by the BiH army. Actually, it was issued by the Defence Secretariat on the 5th of June, 1995. Since it was issued on the 5th of June, 1995, we see that in the third paragraph it says that they processed what they received in the month of May 1995. There's a reference to food, materiel, technical equipment, and fuel. Those were issued to military units in the region of Tuzla. It also says here in the penultimate paragraph -- it's not very legible in B/C/S, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you said "technical equipment." Could you just guide us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's the first -- it's the first row in English, "technical," the last word in first line, and then "equipment" goes in the second line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And in the list, where do we find technical equipment in the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I cannot find it in the list either, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- but it is mentioned in the first sentence. What they meant, I don't know. But obviously it was only food enumerated further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, and, of course, oil, which is not food.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, oil as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- a fuel, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes, but perhaps we should have a closer look at it, sometimes it is pasting and copying the part of the text --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I read it. So I couldn't read anything else then it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but of course, you say to the witness that it ... yes, you referred to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What they received and you included technical equipment and it's announced that there was technical equipment which is not in any way then substantiated in what follows. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably it was some kind of form on their side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- where they always include the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There seems to be no disagreement as how to understand. It was announced but it's not specified in any way. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will read in English since I cannot read B/C/S version. It's very hard. We had to enlarge it very much to be able to read it, so the witness can actually have translated back. The last -- the second-last paragraph says: "We wish to note that the above quantities have been separated out of the humanitarian aid contingent which arrived in the area through UNHCR, while some of the food was obtained from the Dutch battalion."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kralj, we have already discussed your knowledge about the food that UNHCR delivered to civilians, and some of it ended up with soldiers as well. Did you know that the Dutch battalion also supplied the BiH army with food?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Department for Civilian Affairs, i.e., Colonel Djurdjic, was told that the Dutch battalion did supply the units of the 28th Division of the BiH army which were deployed in Srebrenica with food and sometimes with fuel as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D723, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D723 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next document on our screen, we should have 1D2226.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kralj, this is a document issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 2nd of July, 1994. It says here that the number of Military Observer teams and other specialised teams is increasing by the day, and the movement of convoys and teams from the UNPROFOR command for the former BH is badly planned. The decision-making responsibilities in the UN command tend to overlap. In your work, did you come across problems due to the lack of efficiency in UNPROFOR command, and did that result in problems with convoy transports?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was composed of several and various national contingents. As a result, UNPROFOR had problems in terms of commanding those contingents because some commanders obeyed their own national bodies or representatives of the countries they came from, and that did result in certain tensions and problems. Some of them even tried to carry out some intelligence work for their own countries. This was particularly pronounced among -- among Military Observers who frequently moved around without any purpose across the territory of Republika Srpska, most commonly in the direction of Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D724, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D724 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic, returning to the previous document and the issues I raised, is there any chance that an abbreviation is used in the original MTS which stands for a category rather than a description of -- of specific goods? MTS, I do understand, is a general --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- abbreviation for --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's how I understand it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- categories of goods and that could --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But it's technical goods, MTS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you only provide food, the food would still be MTS because it is part of that conglomerate which is usually referred to as MTS which, by the way, also could -- materiel and technical goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it is more military term. Maybe we could use presence of the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I just noticed that and that indeed it is very difficult to read, but it seems that MTS is -- I even see "Brane MTS," the word before that, in the original. I'm -- I'm talking about the previous document. Please proceed. I just wanted to -- to see whether we can get further clarification as to -- or further explanation as to why the one term is used and why, in the specification, we do not find anything else than oil and food. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, talking about terminology, could MTS also encompass food, foodstuffs?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those are two totally separate categories. Food is part of headquarter -- headmaster and MTS encompasses everything including technical equipment, generators, vehicles, weapons, and ammunition. This is a military term, a very general military term, and describes technical equipment of military purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that "headmaster" is probably better translated as "quartermaster."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of your suggestion. You know, Mr. McCloskey, that the usual way of dealing with any translation issue is to ask our interpreters to verify the accuracy and not to give them already the better translation. That's -- but I leave it to that for the time being. There seems to be no great confusion about the matter, but I'm very much attached to the proper procedure in dealing with translation issues. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Then we need the next document, 1D2229, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kralj, what we have before us is a document issued by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on 30th November 1992. First of all, in the 1st Corps, did you receive this document and is this visible in the document itself?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows that it was sent to the commander himself, which is not commonplace. Where you see that it says the command of 1 KK, that's the command of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the last page, we see the signature of Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since we have now inspected this, let us go back to the first page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On line 1, it says -- the exact date is blurred. We don't know when that happened. However, the report was drafted on the 30th of November and it says: "In November 1992, an unannounced UNPROFOR convoy arrived, including 19 vehicles ..." It says further on, line 8 in B/C/S, line 6 in English: "The citizens of Bratunac prevented the passage of the convoy to Srebrenica ..." After that, the convoy was sent to Bajina Basta from where it attempted to go to Srebrenica through Skelani. After that, it says that: "Citizens of Bajina Basta, Skelani and other places in the vicinity participated in preventing the passage of the humanitarian aid convoy." Do you know that such spontaneous reactions of citizens towards UNPROFOR convoys did happen, especially at the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was a period of intense activities. And the citizens were still not properly informed about the role of UNPROFOR, and every time an armed unit entered with equipment, weapons and ammunition, it was perceived as international assistance to Muslims, and they protested vehemently. So, at first, it was a huge problem. But then when the system was well established, owing to political bodies and the highest political leadership of Republika Srpska, some order was installed into letting UNPROFOR vehicles enter the enclaves and stay in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we see the following page in B/C/S. And we should stay on the same page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the top of the page, at the beginning of that paragraph which is the third paragraph in the English version on page 1, it says: "Through the engagement of the Republika Srpska Army Main Staff and the Drina Corps, as well as the influence of the president of the Presidency, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, and the authorities, the citizens of the aforementioned places understood the situation, and after inspection, the convoy passed and arrived in Srebrenica unimpeded." Along your lines of command, what were you told? Were you told to allow the passage of convoys that were approved and that allowed inspection or to obstruct their passage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I put a two-folded question, I mean, whether you were instructed this or something opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The question was what were you instructed not give him two -- only two choices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I could rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase your question, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard the question, Mr. Kralj, but let's drop what I asked you. I will not insist on an answer at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If may I just ask you, Mr. Lukic, is page 28, from line 4 to 8 -- to 7, don't they answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He, actually, yes, anticipated my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So your question is answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, perhaps for our understanding of this document, I take it that for a proper understanding it's important to know what the ethnicity was, what the dominant ethnicity was, of the populations in -- in Bratunac, Bajina Basta, and -- isn't it? In order to properly understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having read this document, Witness, could you tell us whether this, as it was qualified by Mr. Lukic as -- as a spontaneous protest against letting through the convoys by the local population, was that a Serb protest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was a protest of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That may be obvious for those involved, but it's clear hereby. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would just tender this document at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we just see again whose name is at the bottom so we understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was shown it was General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was shown to the witness. Then in the absence of any objections, Mr. Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D725, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D725 is admitted into evidence. Witness, the document also talks about the position taken by Mr. Izetbegovic in opposing letting the convoys through and the purposes for that position, at least the aim he apparently wanted to achieve. Do you know where that information comes from? Do you have details about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objective of Alija Izetbegovic was to create confusion and to portray --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question was: What is the source for this information as we find it here in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The source is always the intelligence organs of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do you know what they observed to draw this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time there were attempts to reach agreement, to talk, but Alija always wanted to blame the Serb side as much as possible. So anything that could have caused -- anything that would work against the army or the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's a rather general statement. What I was seeking, whether had you any specific information such as the leadership on that day had a telephone conversation with, or whatever. But detailed information which is at the source of this conclusion --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any specific information about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time you were in the 1st Corps, November 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us look at 1D2232.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document of the Main Staff. The name of General Ratko Mladic is type-signed. And it says that he orders, in paragraph 1: "Enable unhindered passage and protection of consignments, equipment and personnel providing aid intended for the civilian population of the opposing side." Paragraph 4 states: "Ensure that all units and the entire army personnel are acquainted with this order and complying with it." Were you informed about this order in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed about this order, and from the commander personally, we received an order to provide information within the scope of our own work to our personnel who were involved in control. And paragraph 4 shows that it is necessary to ensure that all units, not only at corps level but lower-ranking units as well. The entire personnel of the army should be familiarized with this order and that they should comply with it. It is signed by General Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D726, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D726 is admitted into evidence. I have one question for you, Mr. Kralj. This document, in giving four instructions of a rather general nature, were they helpful in performing your tasks or in performing the tasks by the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, if a document is signed by General Mladic, the soldiers of the units would take that as the gospel. This was carried out to the letter, and there was no question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They would strictly abide by that, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, could I ask you, do you know the difference between Protocol I and Protocol II to the Geneva Conventions? What is Protocol I mainly dealing with and what is Protocol II mainly dealing with? Could you explain that? Because if you want to abide -- strictly abide by that, that at least assumes some understanding of what you are instructed to do. Could you tell us what the main purpose of Protocol I and the main purpose of Protocol II is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a matter of fact, we organised training about Protocol I and Protocol II in the corps units. Right now, I could not -- it's not clear to me. I do not find the difference between the two to be clear to me. Although I did deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where did you deal with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It pertained to POWs, the civilian population ... as a matter of fact, I attended a course in San Marino [Realtime transcript read in error "some marina"] for 15 days about international law of war. But I seem to be getting senile, a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't confirm that immediately, Mr. Kralj, but I leave it to that. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can shortly see 65 ter 24847, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kralj, on the roads of Republika Srpska, during the course of one day, would there usually be one convoy or several convoys on the road?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the course of one day on the roads of Republika Srpska, there would always be several convoys. And not only convoys but also individual vehicles. So that movement, among other things, made regular traffic more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see 16 convoys here, Sarajevo-Kiseljak for the most part, but 9 is Kiseljak-Srebrenica and then 11 is Sarajevo-Zepa. All of that envisaged for the 30th of March, 1995. At the time you were in the Main Staff. Is it customary to have General Milovanovic's signature on such documents as well?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is customary that General Milovanovic would sign documents with this kind of content, especially when they are being sent to the UNPROFOR command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From your experience, how many trucks would there be in a single convoy, on average?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, do you have any time --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, we are talking about 1995, I would say -- in regard of this document. And the gentleman was in the Main Staff at that time, so I --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In March 1995, how many trucks you could expect in -- in one convoy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: About ten trucks. On average.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many pages? Can we get an idea? I think this ask a very lengthy document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are other pages, but every single convoy is only explained what it includes. We can go through every single page if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No. I don't suggest that. But I suggest before it's authenticated into evidence, there should be at least something besides the cover page discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's have the next page on our screens. And first, if we can notice number 1. Okay. Number 1 from that list is actually that same number we can find on this page. So the convoy number 30-401/03 ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's document, page 3 in the English, about -- with the same number, 401/03.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It would save time if he discussed briefly this one page. I wouldn't have to go back to it, and I think it would lay the proper foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Here, we have the same number in the first line and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we have the same documents in both English and Serbian? It doesn't look like they are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's just cover page in English. Actually, it is the same. The same number. Only it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes, but it's a convoy --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Everything is not translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- for a person rather than for any delivery of goods, so if the -- if your focus is on convoys for delivery of goods, then you would find on page 3 in the English version which corresponds with -- I think -- I don't know why -- I'm wondering, as a matter of fact, whether the pages do correspond at all, but let's have a look. No, apparently what appears is not corresponding, because the one first follow-up page in B/C/S gives a lot of -- gives a lot of names, et cetera, and this may be a -- but certainly is not the same is what immediately follows in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or at least it's not a -- it could be an incomplete -- it's an incomplete translation, I see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Incomplete, yes, something was skipped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there's a lot skipped. And it is not about the -- the purpose of the journey is that someone is to attend a meeting with a commander of UNPROFOR BH command. Now if we're focussing on delivery of goods, then this may not be a very helpful example, Mr. Lukic, if that's your purpose. Of course, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's see --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The Prosecution, for authentication, would be fine if we just focussed a bit -- just on the process which --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I like to try with the next document, maybe it is translated. We would call 24858, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean with the next document, not the next convoy or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next document. Did I say "convoy"? Sorry, it's document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're abandoning this document, not tendering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not tendering it since some confusion arose. We have good backup with this one. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a document of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska here. The date is the 19th of April, 1995. It is sent to the UNPROFOR command by Colonel Miletic. It has to do with 17 convoys. The first convoy has the following number: 20-271/04 from Sarajevo to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's use number 2, since it's to Zepa. So the second -- number 2 is number 20-288/04. So it's from Sarajevo to Zepa. And if we can have the third page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps page 5 in the English seems to correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see the same number, 20-288/04, 18 April 1995. Under 1, it is requested that a Ukrainian battalion could travel from Sarajevo to Zepa. Under 2, purpose of the convoy, food supply. And under 6, we can see the contents or the cargo of the convoy en route to Zepa, personal equipment and weapons. And there's also a list of the foodstuffs that was transported in the convoy. Under 7, it says that the convoy leader would be in possession of cargo specifications and that written approval can be sent to the Military Observers at Pale. This was signed by the chief of the BH command, Major-General Nicolai. And then in handwriting it says: Reduce coffee to 15 kilos and salt to 50 kilos and sugar to 150 kilos. No other reductions were requested. Do you know what UNPROFOR had in Pale?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR had its liaison office manned by Military Observers and interpreters. Through them, it faxed its requests from that office to the sector for civilian affairs in the Main Staff. Then returned information went also by fax from the Main Staff to that office at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is another convoy, that one to Gorazde and another one to Sarajevo. And under 12, from Kiseljak to Gorazde. Under 13, from Kiseljak to Gorazde. Then from Srebrenica to Banja Koviljaca several convoys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to try to simplify this. Could -- to properly authenticate this document and to save some time so I don't have to, the original Serbian has some handwriting on it and some and -- and initials. If we could have the witness explain what that is, then you'll understand what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you accommodate Mr. -- otherwise --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kralj, at the very top of the page, it says "yes" in Cyrillic and it is encircled. Next to it is an initial, and then in brackets it says -- it says "restriction." Do you recognise the handwriting? Do you know who approved those convoys and how that was done?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the handwriting and initial of General Mladic. At the top of the document where it says "yes," there is an initial next to the encircled word.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Whose initial did you say this was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic's. His initial.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note this document and as we see in the English, there's a -- the forward brackets with a "probably" written. That is part -- that is a speculation, I believe, by the translator which should not be part of this document. And I don't think the Defence did that. I think this is probably a Prosecution document. But that is not meant to -- it really shouldn't be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you then take care that you have a revised version. And, of course, this is different from what we dealt with recently because this has got nothing to do with a translation in the context of the text, and that's what we talked about earlier, Mr. Lukic, you'll certainly remember. But this is an exegesis of whose initial that is, and if it would be an M, then there's still a lot of persons in this world whose name starts with an M, and that therefore it goes beyond what, as far as matters stand now, I consider to be within the realm of the CLSS. Please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do so, Mr. Lukic, without adding to your problems, I see that the English says convoy number 20-291. The Serbian one says 288. 20-288. Is there anything there that could be done?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I see the same numbers, Your Honour, 20- ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. What was there before --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was changed, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have only one more document. I would tender this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D727, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D727 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And if we just can see 1D2228, and that will be the last document we'll be using with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kralj, the command of the 1st plpbr sent this to the command of the Drina Corps. The signature is that of the commander, Major Rajko Kusic. This is a regular combat report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the signature, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we, yeah, see the bottom part of B/C/S. It's type written, commander Major Rajko Kusic. [Interpretation] Let's go back to the first page. We are interested in bullet point 3 which is on page 1, both in English -- and in B/C/S it is on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says here: "Ukrainian convoy number 07-012/07 comprising three vehicles from Sarajevo to Zepa passed through the check-point in Rogatica. A UNHCR convoy from Karakaj to Zepa, which arrived at the check-point yesterday, is still in Rogatica undergoing a detailed search since ammunition for small arms was found in the convoy yesterday." Let me ask you this: The fact that ammunition or weapons were found, did that slow down the movement of the convoys which followed in the days after such discovery?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discovery of ammunition in convoys did, in a certain way, increase and intensify the control at check-points. It did not influence the passage of the convoys themselves. The only thing that happened was that people at the check-points were more diligent in trying to discover hidden places where ammunition and weapons could be found.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We would just tender this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and that concludes our direct examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D728, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D728 is admitted into evidence. Witness, can you tell us, having looked at this document a second ago, could you tell us anything about the quantity of ammunition that was found in this convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small quantity of ammunition. Several crates of small-arms ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. For such small quantities, was a complaint lodged at the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a protest was indeed lodged with the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And specifically also in relation to this convoy? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, specifically in relation to this convoy, a protest note was lodged with the UNHCR. Political bodies were not at all happy with the fact that ammunition turned up in those convoys, and especially the permanent state committee on co-operation with international organisations that was located in Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Addressing both parties, if that complaint would be available, and if any response - if there's any - by the UNHCR would be available, then it might assist the Chamber in its assessment in evaluation of this piece of evidence. I leave it to that for the time being. Mr. McCloskey, I think we would better start with the cross-examination after our break. Witness, we'll take a break first. And we'd like to see you back, Mr. Kralj, in 20 minutes from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at ten minutes past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I interrupt before Mr. McCloskey begins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, one second, please. Do we need -- well, if the witness arrives, we'll see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to do this before the witness arrives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's intervention regarding the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 33, line 12, it was recorded -- recorded: "I attended a course in some marina ..." The witness said "San Marino," in Italy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So if you want, you can check it with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And one more thing. With the help of Ms. Stewart, our English translation of the D720, MFI, is uploaded. So I can give you the doc number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please provide that document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's doc ID 1D170252.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Registrar hereby is invited to attach that and is given permission to attach that to D720 MFI. Any objection against admission, Mr. McCloskey? Not. D720 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Witness, you'll be cross-examined now by Mr. McCloskey. But before we start that, I asked you a question about Protocol I and Protocol II and you said you followed courses on international law of warfare. A similar question as before about Protocol I and Protocol II. Could you explain to me more or less what subject matter is mainly dealt with in the -- in the Convention on the Laws and Customs of War on Land and the Geneva Conventions? Could you tell me what the difference in subject matter is between those two? Because both are mentioned in the order by General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The convention deals with the way wars are waged. Whereas the protocols provide specific details as to how civilians should be treated, as well as prisoners of war, civilian facilities, the use of military force in certain types of military activities, and so on and so forth. It says there that the military force used should not be exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you say "the convention deals with." I think I referred to two different conventions. On the one hand side, the Convention on Laws and Customs and War on Land and, on the other hand, the Geneva Conventions. When you referred to "the convention," which convention or conventions did you have on mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The convention on land war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now as far as the Geneva Conventions are concerned, are they also dealing with similar matters and then the protocols dealing with details of how to treat civilians and prisoners of war, or do the Geneva Conventions deal with other matters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They deal with other matters as well, such as the obligations of the state signatories of the convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's true for every convention, isn't it? If you conclude a convention, it always deals with what you are obliged to do under that convention. Do you have any further details about the Geneva Conventions compared to, on the one hand, Protocol I and Protocol II and, on the other hand, the convention on the -- on the warfare, land warfare?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Geneva Conventions deal with the customs of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They deal with the customs of war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the laws of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did you retire from your military positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey is counsel for the Prosecution, and you'll find him to your right. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Kralj.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, is it -- it's true, is it not, that in 2008 you came here as a Defence witness and testified in the case of General Miletic, who was on trial with General Gvero and others?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you also came here as a Defence witness for General Tolimir and testified in his trial in 2012?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you aware that both those indictments generally involved Srebrenica and Zepa allegations?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And most recently you testified as a Defence witness in the trial against President Karadzic here.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we understand from your statement and what has already been said that you took formal training in English. Do you still read English and speak it fluently?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as is perfectly appropriate, are you taking time to actually read what you are seeing in front of you on the -- on the screen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have enough time to read both. I read the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm talking about the transcript that you would see that is only in English as it's going in front of you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read it and understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, yes, and I understand -- and there's nothing wrong with reading it. I'm just trying to understand if you, in fact, are reading the questions as they come out in English or you're just listening, which is fine.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I listen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you also read, that was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there's no Serbian transcript on your screen, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, okay, I'm reading on the left-hand screen. I had misspoken. I meant the two documents on the right-hand side screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we saw you were looking from a short distance at your right-hand screen. I do understand that on the right-hand screen the documents shown to you are to be found; whereas on the left screen you have the transcript, in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the left-hand side, I see the transcript, and I've been following the cursor. Once the typing stops, then I start speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's highly appreciated. Especially by our interpreters. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now not long ago, Mr. Lukic showed you an order that was sent out by General Mladic and we saw his name on it, and you responded on page 32, lines 15 through 18, basically saying that this order would be considered gospel by the VRS troops and that they would follow it. Would the same be true of oral orders issued by General Mladic to his troops? Would those orders be considered gospel and would they follow it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska operates on the principle of subordination. And orders of superior officers, especially General Mladic, his orders were strictly adhered to and carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, now you have -- the real issue raised by Mr. McCloskey was whether what you said about written orders, whether the same would be true for oral orders. Could you specifically answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no difference between a written order and an oral order. An order is an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we saw on a document that was just on the screen, it was one of those UNPROFOR requests for convoy passages, and we saw on the Serbian, you identified General Mladic's initial as saying "yes." Was that -- did that mean to approve that particular convoy document that we saw?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That meant that he was made aware of this document and that he approves that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for UNPROFOR requests, was General Mladic's final word final, or did this document go somewhere else for more approvals?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards UNPROFOR, General Mladic's word was final.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
