utterances.text: And you have described the procedure in your statement, and I won't go through that. But I will summarise briefly in that General Mladic played a critical role in that entire process, did he not? And I'm talking about UNPROFOR requests.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From time to time, he would take a look at certain documents and give his approval. It wasn't compulsory for all documents to be submitted, especially if he was not there physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to your statement, which is D712, and I'd like to take you to what should be page 10 in the English. It's paragraph 25. And in looking at this first paragraph, we see: "Towards the end of 1994, I was transferred to the Main Staff." Was that on the 8th of November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a bit before the 8th of November, 1994, because that day is my Patron Saint's Day. I think it was on the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The 4th of November, 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. It goes on to say that: "I was assigned to interpret from English to Serbian in the same sector as General Milos Djurdjic, who was the chief of the Department for Co-operation with international military forces and I should think also with humanitarian and certain other international organisations." So we hear you saying that: "I should think that he was also with humanitarian and certain other international organisations."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 31499. And it should be page, let's say, 24 in e-court. And if we could go to the bottom of the page. I'm sorry, this should be 26 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you'll see that Mr. Vanderpuye has asked you a question and you must be looking at one of the convoy requests. And he says: "And we can see here the word 'ne' in a circle with a question mark and then crossed out. And I am sure you don't have a specific" - then let's go to the next page - "recollection of this document because it's been a while, but next to the circle with a crossed out, the 'ne' appears to be a 'da' in Cyrillic [sic]."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What I'd like to do is go to page 25 in the -- in the e-court. And could we go to the page before that so I can get the question. I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The question is: "Okay, Colonel Djurdjic, your boss, also participated in this" - and then let's go to the next page - "process; right? And your answer is: "The colonel was the most competent person in the chain. Not the chain, really, but he had the best expert knowledge of all in the Main Staff when it came to humanitarian aid and UNPROFOR convoys. He also held the greatest responsibility." Do you stand by that answer that you gave to Mr. Vanderpuye in the Tolimir case?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So why in your statement did you make this comment: "... and I should think also with humanitarian and certain other international organisations"?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since we compiled this statement with the lawyer, an effort was made to keep it shorter, the statement, and probably this was an omission. I would say and I would like to add with humanitarian organisations as well. Maybe it's just a mistake in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you read your statement after you made it to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did read it, I signed it, and there's no major difference there. We did that kind of work too, with humanitarian organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you've stated that while you were liaison officer for the 1st Krajina Corps, that the UN people that were moving in the area were doing recon on the area. You also mentioned that you thought they were doing recon for future bombing runs. And can you tell me, did you, as the chief liaison officer at the 1st Krajina Corps and the liaison officers that you had been dealing with the brigade, did you also keep track of the movement of those UN personnel and report back intelligence information about their movements or about any other interesting information to your commanders or to your intelligence officers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We provided our information to our immediate superior. Usually we were the ones who received from the intelligence service the information that our check-points had missed, if I can put it that way, without us noticing, that there were certain activities that these persons were carrying out or that there was something in relation to the equipment that they were carrying. So we were warned about that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can barely hear the witness due to background noise. Could all unnecessary microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think I'm the guilty party on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, your microphone may be necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness -- if it's background noise, would it assist in any way if the witness would come a bit closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is the microphone of anyone else who is not speaking at the moment when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you could try to switch off, Mr. McCloskey, when you are not speaking. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Colonel, you did monitor these groups for any information that may be interested for you -- to your command.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was a Military Observer as well during my military career. I was a Military Observer of the United Nations, and I knew full well what the procedure was and the system of work of the United Nations as well, especially Military Observers and others who were there to provide humanitarian aid and were in that function in Republika Srpska. It's not that I particularly followed them, but I knew what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So the question was: Did you get information that you thought may be of interest to your command about these groups and report back to them about it, to your command?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did the brigade liaison officers, who would have been under your supervision, do that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had only one check-point in Gradiska for entering the 1st Corps area. That is how humanitarian convoys from Zagreb came. They had different experts. They had metal detection experts, security experts, intelligence experts, that is to say, personnel was chosen that can perform such functions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm stopping you because I have great difficulties in understanding how what you're tell us is in answer to the question. What Mr. McCloskey would like that know simply is whether you used your position as a liaison officer and the liaison officers that were subordinate to you, whether you also used your position in order to gather information about UNPROFOR, where they moved, what they did, et cetera? Did you gather that kind of information and report it to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I followed UNPROFOR convoys from the moment they crossed the border until they left the territory. So of course I'd report how the convoy went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that limited to convoys or was that about other information as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Limited to convoys only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the question was about the officers. You said you didn't do that personally. Now you told the Judge something --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've now said that you did do it. You had previously told me that you personally didn't do it. My question was: Did your liaison officers in the brigades of the 1st Krajina Corps report on not just the movements but other interesting intelligence-type information that may be of interest to their commands?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that had to do with UNPROFOR activities and movement and that of humanitarian organisations, check-points, responsible persons, the chain of command was there to send this information up. The check-point would report to its superior brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll try one last time, Colonel. I understand that they would have reported on the movement and where they went and when they went there. What I'm asking you about is intelligence information. Things that -- people that are on there, when they stop, what they get out and are doing, anything that would be interesting to the command. Intelligence-type information. You know what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If UNPROFOR would stop somewhere and take some pictures and if some of the people that were there and that were in charge would see that, of course they would report on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. McCloskey is thinking about whether UNPROFOR members in their -- in their own time would drink too much or would do kind of things that would -- was there any such -- Mr. McCloskey, is that the kind of -- otherwise be more specific in your questions and give a few examples of what you mean and then the witness can confirm or deny that such or similar information was gathered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If which go to 65 ter 31503. We can deal with this matter very simply, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the issue apparently is were you just liaising or were you spying on them as well. Is that the simple question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you spying on them as well, Witness? Before you continue to read, could you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Liaison officers did not spy. They just monitored. They monitored what those people did, where they went, why they went where they went, on how many occasions. This is not spying. If you observe that somebody is going somewhere for the fifth time, to the same location, and takes photos there, why, you wonder. In view of the fact that the location has an important military facility, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take look at the -- this simple document before us. It's from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps on the 12th of September, 1993, when you were the liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry. Thank you very much. 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you were the liaison officer. And it's to the command of the 1st OKbr, the Armoured Brigade, and the 43rd Infantry Motorised Brigade, and Major Slavko Kralj. That's you; right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see that that first paragraph, "with regard to the movement and control of UNPROFOR observers through our territory," and it gives a list of places, including on the Prijedor axis, through these two zones, and then the bottom of the page it says: "Patrols shall be allowed within the boundaries of the permitted area." Turning the page in English: "Every crossing of the river Sava and entry onto the territory must be announced in good time and met with and escorted by our liaison officer." "Liaison officers shall inform the commands of the 1st OKbr and 43rd pmbr of where they are going, when they will return, and of anything else they observe while on the move which would be of interest to the commands." So, Colonel, this was an order to you to observe these folks and get back to your command with anything of interest. And that would include intelligence information, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps if you will allow me, I'd like to explain this document. The 1st Krajina Corps withdrew from Slavonia pursuant to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel Kralj, you need to answer the question first and then a fair explanation is always possible. But answer my question, please.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally with these monitors, they couldn't enter the territory of Republika Srpska if they were not escorted by me. To control that agreement in certain zones that were set out in the agreement, my obligation was to report on their conduct and behaviour, what else they did in addition to the activities that were planned. As a liaison officer, I simply submitted my reports on the work of those UN monitors whose mission was to inspect areas south of the Sava, several kilometres in the depth of territory from the river. And they didn't need an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you give a very long answer and you're circling around what apparently the question is. That is, to report on anything they observe while on the move and that would be of interest of the commands, which is to be reported. That does not exclude intelligence information, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Every piece of information may be welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the answer is yes, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it may be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Took us a while to come there. If you would be a bit more direct in answering the questions. Carefully listen to them and answer them, rather than to spend a lot of words on matters which are only in the margin. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry for interrupting you, but then can we have the definition what intelligence data is. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's everything, it doesn't exclude intelligence. I mean everything is everything, Mr. Lukic. So I do agree with you that -- and I think that I already earlier, when Mr. McCloskey said you know what I understand when he was referring to intelligence, that I certainly encouraged him to come with examples so that there would be no misunderstanding about what Mr. McCloskey considers to be intelligence and what the witness -- but now we are at the point, if nothing is excluded, intelligence is also not excluded. Everything. Please proceed. And you move on forwards far quicker, Mr. McCloskey, if you would phrase the questions in such a way that the witness just has no opportunity to -- to find the sidelines. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is a secret I have been trying to find, Your Honour, for many years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, try again, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I will keep trying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you have seen documents that showed that the -- some ammunition came in through UNHCR convoys, that food came in through UNHCR convoys that managed to find its way to the army, you have testified that the UN forces were conducted reconnaissance, including reconnaissance for bombing. In 1995, when you were in the Main Staff, as far as you knew, did the Main Staff consider UNPROFOR in the eastern enclaves to be the enemy because of these activities?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that UNPROFOR considered the Main Staff as their enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was the opposite, I think. Did you, was -- in the Main Staff, was UNPROFOR considered to be your enemy, in terms of the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think that the -- the answer was the opposite, actually. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, the answer as translated? Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The answer was translated wrongly. But I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least you would seek verification of that. Could you -- could you again answer the question whether you, that is, the VRS Main Staff, considered UNPROFOR to be your enemy in terms of the armed conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you consider the siphoning off or the taking of some humanitarian aid from convoys a reason to restrict or -- excuse me, a reason to restrict that aid to the eastern enclaves in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, partly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you acknowledge, then, that there were restrictions placed on those enclaves in 1995 for humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Restrictions were not imposed on the enclaves. But we bore in mind how much UNPROFOR needed for the normal functioning. I mean, how much of the different types of commodities and goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, I'll try again because we saw your answer before that. Did you restrict the humanitarian aid to the enclaves because some of it was getting siphoned off to the army?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we are dealing with linguistic issues rather than anything else. In view of the answers you've given at this moment, Witness, could I ask you the following: Were you allowing less humanitarian aid in than requested because you had information that part of the humanitarian aid ended up with the BiH armed forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your mind, as an officer and a JNA officer before that, would you have been justified in doing because of what was happening?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are superior bodies which discussed that, and I mean a joint military commission. The omissions of that kind were discussed as well as all the problems that arose either from working with humanitarian organisations or UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not an answer to the question. Witness, I would really urge you to answer the questions because, otherwise, we're unable to properly evaluate the evidence you are giving. Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will try this question again. But this time I want to use UNPROFOR as the example. There have been mention here of the occasional times where an UNPROFOR convoy may have had contraband or material on it. Do you, as an officer, believe that those violations, as would you have seen them, justified you in restricting the supplies to the UNPROFOR troops?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean, Witness, because that's what it all turned around, that you granted all the requests without any limitations for whatever UNPROFOR asked to be brought in in convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't approve things, but there were certain restrictions, as shown by the documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you have been asked seven times about whether there were restrictions. You said no, no, no. And now you say, of course, there were restrictions. Let's try to -- to get to the answers a bit more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Colonel, the simple point I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The question was not about restrictions but what he thinks and is that reasonable and justified. That was the question. What is his position. Not whether there were restriction --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I object --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- Mr. Lukic, that was some of the questions but there were other questions which clearly asked for whether there any restrictions imposed. Let's move on and let's avoid to make it a discussion about concepts. And Mr. Mladic should not speak at any audible volume. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The simple point that I want to hear your answer on, sir, is that with the occasional infraction or violation from the UNPROFOR convoys or the UNHCR convoys as we've discussed, does that, in your view as a military professional, justify the restrictions on the UNPROFOR and the civilian populations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I'm intervening again. When I earlier said that questions were indeed about justifications, the proper way of dealing with this is, first, to establish whether there were any restrictions, and, second, then whether they were justified. Justified, of course, asking for some opinion and some judgement as well. But the first question is were there restrictions. Because if you ask a witness: Did this and this justify that, then it doesn't answer the question whether that happened at all. So, therefore, the logical and appropriate way is: First, to establish whether there were restrictions. That's the reason why I asked the witness whether the requests were granted. Because if they're not granted, then apparently there are restrictions. They are cut down in one way or another. Could we try to follow this scheme. What happened, why did it happen, and was that justified by other events which may have happened as well. That's, in my view, the appropriate way of tackling the issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, this will work better.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, it's the position of the Prosecution that there were serious restrictions placed on UNPROFOR and humanitarian aid to create great hardship in the enclaves. Would, in your view as a professional officer, such restrictions, if done, be ever justified?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. And it's if this, then that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll help you. Witness -- witness, I'll try to assist you. I think a minute ago you said that restrictions were imposed, restrictions imposed on UNPROFOR and humanitarian aid. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood things correctly. You can see in certain documents that things were not always fully approved during a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Why were they not approved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Primarily if there was combat going on in a certain part, and especially when NATO pact started its air-strike campaigns, then convoys did not move because they had not been approved. Those were the main reasons, as far as I know, why some convoys were suspended or not approved ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, suspension for practical circumstances is not the same as not being approved. Before any air-strikes, was it merely combat activity that caused the Main Staff not to approve convoys?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, only ongoing combat was the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be at the time when the convoy would pass, not at the point in time when it was requested if situations were then different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the situation changed, convoys were approved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, but ... so only practical circumstances were at the basis of not -- denying convoys to pass through. Then we -- at least we started with the facts, Mr. McCloskey. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P1469 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. McCloskey, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to tender this, that document, 65 ter 31503.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P6855, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if we could have P1469.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This first page is a letter from General Milovanovic enclosing a document called Directive 7: "Directive for further operations, op number 7." And it's sent out 17 May 1995. This is a document you've seen in two other appearances before this Tribunal; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 14 in the English, page 21 in the Serbian. Under the section of support for combat operations, moral and psychological support. Let's go down to the fourth paragraph and we'll all recall that this was -- came out in the name of Supreme Commander, Dr. Radovan Karadzic. "The relevant state and military organs responsible for work with UNPROFOR and the humanitarian organisations, shall, through the planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits, reduce and limit the logistics support of UNPROFOR to the enclaves and the supply of material resources to the Muslim population, making them dependant on our goodwill while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and the international -- and international public opinion."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, sir, you and Colonel Djurdjic were part of the Main Staff office that was responsible for the work of UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. First of all, Colonel Djurdjic was responsible, and I, at the time when he was absent, deputised for him or assisted him. In other words, my main task was as an interpreter. If Djurdjic was absent, I could deal with documents in terms of pure handling and administrative handling of such a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, you were part of the Department of Civilian Affairs in the Main Staff, and you and Mr. Djurdjic dealt specifically with this subject: UNPROFOR and humanitarian convoys; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: A correction: Mr. Djurdjic. And when he was absent, then I had to stand in for him or replace him to deal with certain paperwork.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, so you dealt with him. You, in his absence, and if Mr. Djurdjic was there, he did it. So, therefore, again, the simple answer is yes, but perhaps -- it was no one else. It was you -- your department which dealt with those matters, if only administratively.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as you've already testified, Colonel Djurdjic's superior was General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So General Mladic and Colonel Djurdjic would have been responsible for following this supreme directive; correct? What I just read.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about this directive only here. I've already told you that. This was a level of confidentiality that was way above me. I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards your question, General Mladic is responsible for the implementation of this directive, if it was sent to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And General Mladic would have -- who would he have ordered to implement it? Who was his top man for convoys? And if it will help refresh your recollection, I read you back what -- how important you said Mr. Djurdjic was. Who would Mladic have assigned this task to?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would have assigned it to Colonel Djurdjic who was a member of this state body for humanitarian aid on behalf of the Ministry of Defence and the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And he was the chief of the administration for civilian affairs in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who was the one person that helped him get his job done, Djurdjic? Who was the one person that Djurdjic had to rely on to help him get his job done?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did most of the work by himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's, again, not an answer to the question. Do you know of anyone closer to Mr. Djurdjic who would take over if he was absent? Closer -- I mean anyone closer than you were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was the closest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's break time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We'll take a break, Witness. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes from now. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, questions which are not of a composite nature and questions that are primarily aiming and establishing facts and not dealing too quickly with opinion, judgement, et cetera, may assist in getting the evidence you apparently are seeking in a more efficient way. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I respond briefly to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a question as a matter of fact. It was a suggestion. Think about it. If you think it would, then I say it may assist. If you consider that it doesn't assist, then you put the questions in the way you would -- it was just a serious effort to see whether I could -- whether I could assist you in achieving as quickly as possible what you - as far as we understand - are seeking to achieve at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President, and I was going to attempt to see if I could convince you that opinion and such may be -- may be important, but I very much appreciate being alerted to what you think is the most important. That's critical to both parties. And I thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We take a break, and we resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're just -- we'll finish up with Directive 7. It should be on your screen. And we've gone over that particular paragraph. I won't ask you what you think of it. But you're a career JNA soldier. You know about the full method of creating and putting together an important document such as a directive, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I never attained that level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've seen this document several times. Tell us who actually drafted this directive, these pages that contain this, among other?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the end of the document in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I was hoping to -- well, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: From your memory, please, if possible, sir, unless you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is written here that this was drafted by Radivoje Miletic, but I have no idea whether he actually did do that or when.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you testified for Radivoje Miletic and -- so you must have known that he -- as you testified, that he had drafted it, at least after the war. Or have you forgotten that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never testified that he was the one who authored that. That must be a mistake. How can I testify about something that I don't know of?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will skip that. I don't know what the problem there is. I didn't say that to you. So we'll just skip that. Did you know that in a document like this, that it's put together by the very organs of the Main Staff that are responsible for the various parts of it, intel, morale, legal, religious, logistics, that it's a joint effort of the Main Staff bodies responsible for this content?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know of that document or in the way in such a document is compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution's position, sir, that what is stated here about "through planned and unobtrusively restrictive issuing of permits," et cetera, that that is precisely what happened. That President Karadzic's orders, directive, were followed by the Main Staff, and we saw the results on the ground. You've testified that you were able to see some of the -- or you were able to learn of some of the results on the ground. You too saw the restrictions and what was happening to the people of UNPROFOR and the people of Srebrenica, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in Srebrenica, and I did not follow that situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, my first suggestion was no composite questions. You introduced five different elements in your question or in your introduction to the question, and then, of course, the witness chooses the one which he prefers to deal with rather than to be focussed by you on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll keep trying, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's speak briefly -- I want to go back briefly to Mladic's involvement in this process that you describe regarding the UNPROFOR convoys. And I want to go something that you said in cross-examination in the Tolimir case, and we can put it on the screen, if need be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 31499. And that should be page 11 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Vanderpuye asked you this question: "He" -- and where he says "he," we can see from above that he means General Tolimir. So: "He, General Milovanovic, and General Mladic needed to know what the disposition of those convoys were in order to frame how to address requests and other issues concerning future convoys; right? And your answer was: "All three of them, as part of their duties, did deal with convoys. General Mladic reviewed each item in detail and would ask for Colonel Djurdjic's suggestions on numerous issues in order to be able to make a proper decision. If General Mladic was not there, the same thing" - next page in e-court - "could be done by General Milovanovic." And then Mr. Vanderpuye asked you: "And if General Milovanovic wasn't there, the same thing could be done by General Tolimir; right, Mr. Kralj?" And your answer is: "Well, he couldn't unless the commander authorised him to do that." So do each of those answers to those questions, did that refer to the kind of convoy requests for UNPROFOR that we had looked at briefly?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly, General Mladic authorised General Milovanovic to deal with questions that pertained to UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations. General Tolimir was in these working groups, these bodies, where he could specifically say what was agreed upon and what was not agreed upon, if there was any dispute. So if General Mladic issued an order, it was compulsory for everyone else. And within the scope of his work, he could consult anyone if he found anything to be unclear. I'm referring to General Mladic, but everything was clear to him more than to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say "him," you mean General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean General Mladic. He had more information about everything, from different sides. Whereas all the rest of us at lower levels, it was for us to act in accordance with his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You state here, you testified under oath, and I quote: "General Mladic reviewed each item in detail and would ask for Colonel Djurdjic's suggestions on numerous issues in order to be able to make a proper decision." So do you stand by that? Did General Mladic review each item in detail on these convoy UNPROFOR requests?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whichever document reached the General, he would look at it carefully, study it, and if he found anything unclear in relation to humanitarian aid, he would require additional information. And he could receive that information only from Colonel Djurdjic because Colonel Djurdjic was the one who precisely had all this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That wasn't the question, Witness. You'd testified that General Mladic, General Milovanovic, and General Tolimir dealt with convoys, and you said: "General Mladic reviewed each item in detail and would ask for Colonel Djurdjic's suggestion on numerous issues in order to be able to make a proper decision." Along those procedural lines, did General Mladic make decisions after having reviewed each item in detail?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And can we offer this bit of the transcript into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, this bit of a transcript, Mr. McCloskey, is a pretty wide request. Perhaps restrictions should apply --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 65 ter 31499, e-court pages 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, I mean do we need the full 92 pages just for the purposes of the two pages we dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, no, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just the two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we reserve a number and you'll upload the relevant pages and they'll then be dealt with under the number. Mr. Registrar, the number to be reserved for an excerpt of the transcript would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P6856, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is reserved for that purpose. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, I want to talk hopefully briefly with you about the process for humanitarian convoys, not UNPROFOR convoys, and we see in your statement that you describe a bit of a different procedure for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can we go to D336. And we'll see that this is a portion of the Official Gazette of the Republika Srpska. It's dated 14 March, which is just a few days after 8 March, when Directive 7 was created. It's 1995. So if we could just go to page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You'll agree with me that this is the law setting up this -- this committee for co-operation?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have testified before that before this law, the VRS had control of the humanitarian convoys; but after this law, this body had control. Is that a simple -- simple statement of the guts of what you've got in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I clarify? This body received requests, initial requests, for the passage of convoys of humanitarian aid and then they would consider them. Milos Djurdjic, Colonel Milos Djurdjic was co-ordinator of that committee with the ministry and the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, apologies for interrupting again, but you say we're looking at a law. What I see is a decision on the appointment of members and the president of a committee, not -- I do not see any law on my screen at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I believe this has the force of law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- and that was my reference to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then it's -- well, I consider a law to be some kind of a general rule, whereas here apparently persons are appointed on this committee. But if that explains the matter, then there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So there was a -- we can see seven people that are on this committee and Milos Djurdjic, your boss, was one of them; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were never persons on this committee [as interpreted], and Milos was number 7 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's correct. And so the answer is yes, that he's one of the seven. And he was in a place to know better than anybody what General Mladic would want to allow in humanitarian -- on humanitarian convoys, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us if General Mladic would not be pleased if this committee set up by Karadzic's government recommended something he didn't want? Is that a fair conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I object at this point of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the base for your objection is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The objection is that this witness should tell us what Mr. Mladic would feel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the objection is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever see Djurdjic or General Mladic complain or get upset with the activity and the approvals of this committee?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the committee would not give approval had Colonel Djurdjic not come with a clear-cut position as to whether the Army of Republika Srpska could secure safe passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that, again, is not an answer to the question. That any --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But that is an answer I'd very much like, Your Honour, for you to understand but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, yes. But do you then still insist on an answer to your question or are you just happy with the testimony as given although unrelated to your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you but I didn't want to let that answer get away. No, I am, and I appreciate your clarification with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it's part of his testimony. Do you still insist on an answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I'll try to -- Witness, did it -- do you have any knowledge about either Mr. Djurdjic or Mr. Mladic expressing that they were unhappy with or that they did not agree with any decision, opinion, or whatever, may have expressed -- may have been expressed by this committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no such knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then you would agree -- you would agree with me that what you said that when Colonel Djurdjic brings the views of the VRS to this committee, that something that the committee is going to take very seriously?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we go back to Directive 7 and we see the order for -- for the restrictive issuing of permits, would -- the committee under that order would be obliged to follow that, the order in Directive 7, would it not?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, whether the committee was made aware of that directive at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not my question. You're a lieutenant-colonel in the VRS. Would this directive from President Karadzic that you have read and seen for many years now, would -- would the convoy approvals of this committee be obligated to be in conformance with that directive?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And with the VRS also following President Karadzic's order in Directive 7, would you -- did you see a co-ordination between this committee and Mr. Djurdjic in the Main Staff to follow the order in Directive 7 to restrict permits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At this point I would object, since this is actually different from the evidence we have in the case. We know about the Directive 7/1 and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Whoa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't say any [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- you're supposed not to put to the witness what we have received as evidence. The question was whether this witness saw any co-ordination and I think he can answer that question, irrespective of what evidence we may have heard at other moments. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Co-ordination in the Main Staff to follow the order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- in the Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's -- you may have --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the pertinent part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may argue -- yes. Mr. Lukic, you may argue about Mr. McCloskey has not presented this as evidence we received. He suggests what he suggests, which is in a leading question permitted, and the matter you're raising is argument rather than an objection to the question. Could you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, or you can deal with the matter in re-examination. But it's usually of no use to discuss with the witness what other evidence may have been presented to this Chamber. Mr. McCloskey, you have had now sufficient time to think again about your question and about how to phrase it in such a way that you get a direct answer. Could you please put the question or a question on the same subject to the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any co-ordination between Mr. Djurdjic, his administration, and this committee in their work related to humanitarian convoy approvals?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, Witness, could I ask you the following. Mr. Djurdjic was a member of that committee. Is that not in itself, by definition, that at least on his personal participation in that committee, that already establishes a certain level of co-ordination, because it's one person, both in the committee and participating in -- in the work of his administration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I understand. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So now we have established there was co-ordination between the work of Mr. Djurdjic and this committee regarding humanitarian convoys; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see that the Professor Nikola Koljevic, the deputy president of the Republika Srpska, is the president of this state committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so, having that in mind, let's go to 65 ter 25113.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an intercept that you may recall Ms. Fauveau, Defence counsel for General Miletic, showing you many years ago. And it's identified as a conversation held on 23 June 1995 between Petko Obucina and Zdravko Tolimir. Can you tell us who Petko Obucina was?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petko Obucina was a member of staff of the office of the president of the republic. I don't know what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was an official for Koljevic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see him on the list of names that we just saw a little while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not the question. The question was whether he was an official for Mr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He worked for him. He told that to Ms. Fauveau years ago.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the president's office staff and co-operated with Koljevic, like I just told you before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at this, we see on line 4 that he introduces himself: "It's Petko Obucina here, from the Pale commission. I would like to speak to General Tolimir." Then it goes down and Petko says, when he gets General Tolimir: "General, I have just received a called from Professor Koljevic." General Tolimir says: "Yes." It says: "He was with the prime minister right now, he will there for another 15 minutes. He was asking for you about the exchange for Srebrenica." Tolimir says: "All right." Obucina says: "He was wondering whether Milos, who is there, could be given the green light and that he allow us to deal with it. Otherwise you should call him." Tolimir says: "The commander gave him approval for what he requested. Milos failed to understand and the commander approved what can go in and out of Srebrenica." Petko says: "Can?" Tolimir says: "Just tell him that." And we see the rest of it confirming that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We may need to go to the next page in the Serbian. I can't quite tell. Yes, thank you. Thank you, Ms. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now it's the view of the Prosecution, sir, that this is Mr. Obucina calling and co-ordinating with General Tolimir about issues related to approvals for Srebrenica. You've talked about this intercept before. Is that your view?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KRALJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I see it's 2.15. I have a few documents. I hope I'll get done within 30 minutes of tomorrow, Your Honour, I hope. I don't know how much time I have used but I think I'm within my time-frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would be surprised if you were not on the basis of the last estimates, but we'll verify. Witness, we'll adjourn for the day, and we'd like to see you back. Mr. Kralj, I'll give you the same instructions as I did yesterday, that is, that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony already given yesterday and today, or whether that is testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that's clear, you may follow the usher, and we'd like to see you back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, just one housekeeping while we're --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we need the witness for what you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the witness already can follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the two transcript pages assigned Exhibit P06858 have now been uploaded into e-court under -- 56, sorry, I need to get glasses. P06856 - now I'm dyslexic - have now been uploaded into e-court under 65 ter 31499A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard of no objections, Mr. Lukic. Therefore, P -- first of all, the Registrar is instructed to link the uploaded 31499A document, link it with the number reserved and therefore provisionally assigned P6856. And P6856 is admitted into evidence. We adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 29th of October, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
